You Probably Don’t Need Microservices

A service boundary should earn its operational cost. Here is how I weigh independent deployment and scaling against the work of running a distributed system.

I watched a 3-person team spend months setting up Kubernetes, Kafka, and a service mesh for an app that could have been a single Spring Boot jar. They were solving infrastructure problems instead of building their product. By the time the architecture was “ready,” they’d burned through half their runway. The product never launched.

I’ve managed 60 microservices in production for a government platform. Kubernetes, ZeroMQ, Kafka, Docker, the whole stack. It was the right call for that project. But that project had multiple teams, independent deployment requirements, and government-scale traffic. Most projects don’t.

Microservices can sound like the obvious next step when a system grows. I would want to know which part of the current architecture is actually holding the team back.

A large company's architecture is useful evidence about its constraints. It is not a requirement for a smaller team.

What Consolidation Cases Actually Show

A useful consolidation case explains which costs disappeared and which capabilities the team kept. It does not establish that every distributed system should become a monolith.

Segment’s account describes consolidating its destination-delivery workers after separate services and dependency management became expensive to maintain. The lesson is specific: isolation had benefits, but their implementation made routine changes too costly.

I would use a case like that to investigate a similar bottleneck, not to estimate my own savings. Data movement, orchestration, release coordination, and failure isolation need to be evaluated in the actual workload.

Istio 1.5 consolidated several control-plane components into istiod. Its maintainers explained that those components were already released and operated together, with limited benefit from separate scaling. This was a packaging decision for the control plane, not a rejection of microservices for the applications using the mesh.

What You’re Actually Signing Up For

When someone says “let’s use microservices,” here’s what they’re really proposing:

Network calls instead of function calls. A remote call adds serialization, transport, queueing, and another possible failure boundary. There is no fixed millisecond penalty: measure the deployment and workload. Serial calls can accumulate latency; parallel fan-out makes the slowest required response important. In our auction platform, the path through bidding, user checks, payment validation, and notifications needed careful attention. A faster individual service would not automatically make the whole request faster.

Distributed debugging. I've spent days correlating logs across services to find a serialization mismatch. Shared types can catch some such errors at build time, but neither a monolith nor a successful compile guarantees compatible behavior. Correlation IDs, structured logs, and traces help reconstruct what happened across independently deployed components. That work needs an owner.

Data integrity crosses a boundary. A relational database still provides transactions and constraints inside each service. The difficulty appears when one business operation needs consistent changes across separately owned databases. A single local transaction can no longer cover the whole operation.

For example, deleting a user does not automatically decide what should happen to records in another service. Some may need deletion, some anonymization, and some retention. The services need an explicit contract and a way to handle delayed or failed processing. Separate data ownership is useful, but it moves some consistency work into the application.

Queries spanning services also need a design. API composition and replicated read models are possible approaches; both bring questions about freshness, pagination, and failure handling. This is a different problem from writing a join inside one database.

Local ACID transactions still exist. For a business operation spanning services, one option is a saga: a sequence of local transactions with explicit recovery or compensating actions. A compensation is not a database rollback, and an external payment is not made atomic merely by moving its caller into a monolith. There is no universal service-count threshold where this becomes unmanageable. The hard part is specifying outcomes when a step, including compensation, fails.

Operations grow with the number of independently running components. Each needs deployment, monitoring, ownership, and recovery decisions. A platform can share much of that machinery, so multiplying services does not imply a fixed staffing ratio. I would price the work our team still has to do, including maintaining that platform.

Testing crosses deployment boundaries. Unit tests remain useful, but they do not establish that independently released consumers and producers agree. Contract checks can catch drift before deployment; integration and end-to-end tests cover different risks. Monoliths need interface and integration tests too, particularly when they call external systems. The difference is how many combinations can be running independently.

Understanding the system takes deliberate work. More components can mean more owners, versions, and failure paths to keep track of. Domain boundaries and documentation help, but a small team still has to operate the result. Service count alone is not a measure of modularity.

Questions I Ask Before Adding a Service

I want a concrete answer to each of these before accepting another independently deployed component.

Deployment:

Which change can this team release independently after the split?

If every release still needs synchronized changes elsewhere, I would examine the boundary before adding deployment machinery.

Domain boundaries:

What have we learned from the working system that makes this a stable boundary?

Operations:

Who owns this service when a dependency times out or a deployment fails?
Which recovery behavior have we actually tested?

Cost:

What measured limitation will this split remove?

These questions are more useful to me than a target service count. The answers can justify a split, or show that a module inside the existing application would do the job.

The Distributed Monolith: The Worst of Both Worlds

A common failure mode is splitting deployment without reducing coupling. Services may require coordinated releases, rely on one another's internal tables, or make every feature span several repositories.

That can leave the team paying for network boundaries while retaining much of the release coordination of a single application.

Warning signs worth investigating:

  • You deploy multiple services together, every time
  • A change in one service requires changes in 3 others
  • Services read or change one another's internal database tables
  • You can’t test one service without spinning up 5 others
  • Your “independent” services call each other synchronously in long chains

None of these signals alone proves the design is wrong. Look for a repeated inability to change, test, and operate a service within a clear contract.

Shopify’s Alternative: The Modular Monolith

Shopify's engineering team described evolving its Rails application into a modular monolith: keeping a shared deployment while establishing clearer component boundaries. It is a useful example of improving modularity without first distributing every module.

Their Packwerk tooling checks static references against package boundaries. It helps enforce architectural rules, but it does not prove that every runtime interaction is independent.

The practical appeal of this approach:

  1. Keep calls within one process where a network boundary offers little benefit
  2. Improve ownership and dependencies without adding a deployment for every module
  3. Leave room to extract a service when an actual operational need appears

A modular monolith needs maintained interfaces and data boundaries. Simply putting everything in one repository does not create those boundaries. Keeping them clear can make a later extraction easier.

When Microservices Actually Make Sense

I have also worked on projects where separate services were worthwhile. My C++ video-system migration describes one of those cases. Here are the kinds of needs I would look for:

Multiple independent teams. We had teams that needed to release on different schedules. Separate services can support that when responsibilities and interfaces are clear; the number of teams alone does not dictate the architecture.

Genuinely different scaling requirements. Our auction engine needed to handle thousands of concurrent bids per second. The document management module needed to serve PDFs occasionally. Scaling them together would have been wasteful. This is a real signal.

Regulatory isolation. Payment processing under banking regulations needed to be isolated from the rest of the system. Separate service, separate audit trail, separate security boundary.

Different technology requirements. If one component genuinely benefits from a different language or runtime. Our real-time bidding engine had different performance characteristics than our reporting module.

You've learned the boundaries. Fowler's Monolith First argument is useful here: early feedback can reveal where the domain divides before network interfaces make those divisions more expensive to change. That is an argument for learning, not a guarantee that any monolith will be easy to split.

The Resume-Driven Development Test

I've been guilty of picking a technology because I wanted to learn it. Seeing Kafka in job listings is a good reason to study it; it is not sufficient reason to add it to a product. I try to separate the learning project from the architecture decision.

The honest test: would I still pick this architecture if it didn’t go on my resume? If the answer is “probably not,” that’s worth pausing on.

Some patterns I’ve seen more than once:

  • Breaking an app into 50 services maintained by 2 developers
  • Deploying Kubernetes for a project with 500 users
  • Adding Kafka when your data flow is request-response
  • Implementing a service mesh for 4 services

None of these are wrong in the right context. But the right context is rarely a startup with 5 engineers and no product-market fit yet.

What I’d Actually Recommend

Start with a monolith. Make it modular. Use clear boundaries: separate modules, defined interfaces, no reaching into another module’s database tables. Enforce boundaries with tooling if your language supports it (Packwerk for Ruby, ArchUnit for Java, module boundaries in Go).

Extract a service when you have a real reason. Not “we might need to scale this independently someday,” but “this component is currently a bottleneck and we need to scale it now.” Not “this team might want to deploy independently,” but “this team’s deployment schedule is blocked by another team every sprint.”

For a small team, I would begin by asking whether one deployable application with clear modules meets today's needs. If it does, independent services need a specific benefit to justify their added work.

If existing services repeatedly change together and their separation adds little useful isolation or scaling flexibility, consolidation is worth testing. Measure delivery time, incidents, resource use, and recovery before and after the change.

Choose boundaries that make the system easier to change and operate. Keep the ones that earn their cost, and revisit the ones that don’t. Updated October 9, 2026: removed an unverified survey statistic and unsupported numerical rules, and clarified the case studies and transaction discussion.

Further Reading

Case Studies:

  • Istio: consolidating the control plane into istiod
  • Segment: Goodbye Microservices
  • Shopify: Deconstructing the Monolith
  • Uber: Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture

Perspectives:

  • Martin Fowler: MonolithFirst
  • DHH: How to Recover from Microservices
  • Kelsey Hightower: Monoliths Are the Future
  • Sam Newman: Monolith to Microservices

Technical references:

  • Chris Richardson: the Saga pattern
  • The Tail at Scale (Jeff Dean, Google)
  • Shopify: enforcing modularity with Packwerk

I’m Burak Hamuryen, a Senior Software Engineer in Berlin with 14+ years of experience building distributed systems, real-time video processing, and cloud-native platforms. More at hamuryen.com.
